name: Dagbani
confidence_why: Hudu 2010 and 2022 and Inusah 2021, the current Dagbani phonologists, hold that Dagbani is a tone language with no word stress and that the syllables Olawsky 1999 called stressed are neither longer nor louder, so Olawsky's penultimate-stress analysis (repeated in van der Hulst and Goedemans 2010) is a real but answered dissent, with the caveat that the acoustic rebuttal rests on a single speaker.

catalog_quote: Inusah 2021: 157-158: 'Olawsky (1999) was the first to claim that Dagbanli marks stress which is largely predictable in the language and notes that Dagbanli stress is correlated with a higher amplitude and longer duration; distinct from tone. On the contrary, (Hudu 2007) shows that the vowels which Olawsky described as stressed are neither longer in duration nor higher in intensity than vowels that are supposed to be unstressed. This assertion supports the widely held view among many linguists (e.g. Hudu 2010) that Dagbanli like other Mabia languages is not stress marking. ... This, Olawsky (1999) observes that Dagbanli does not use diacritics in its orthography, but it is necessary to make use of stress and tone in the phonological description. Stress notion in Dagbanli phonology has been established and proved that stress does not exist in the phonology of the language.' Hudu 2022: 273-274: 'Thus, while the more prominent syllable does not bear stress, the structure of the prosodic foot under discussion in this paper displays other relevant properties of a trochaic foot in stress languages.' Hudu 2022: 287: 'In a non-stress language like Dagbani, headedness can only be determined using these other (non-prosodic) criteria.'

sweep_summary: Dagbani (dagb1246) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Lewis 1999 'Rhythmic ambiguity in the Dagbamba drumming of Ghana', is an unpublished BA Honours thesis in ethnomusicology (University of New England; Glottolog keyword 'Drum communication'; language code auto-assigned from 'dagbamba') — not about word stress, no copy located, priority none. Using material already saved from the earlier reading plus a StressTyp2 v1 check, the picture is: Fisch 1912 (pp. 3-4, first-hand, German) reports the main stress 'mostly on the antepenult', often shifted to the penult by heavy syllables, while conflating it with high tone; Olawsky 1999/2002 claim regular penultimate stress per phonological word (with a final-stress subset) — seen only in Google Books snippets and second-hand citations, full texts unobtainable (LINCOM print; CUP chapter 403; JALL 2004 paywalled); Hudu 2007/2010 (UBC, bot-walled) measured no duration/intensity difference for Olawsky's 'stressed' vowels; Inusah 2021 (pp. 157-158, held by the project) and Hudu 2022 (pp. 274, 287, held by the project) treat Dagbani as a non-stress tone language. Dagbani has no StressTyp2 v1 record. Best first-hand statement read: Hudu 2022 'a non-stress language like Dagbani'. Highest-priority unobtained sources: Olawsky 1999/2002 (the penult-stress claim) and Hudu 2010 (the acoustic refutation). all lookups were by direct URL/API.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The literature is split. The reference grammar (Olawsky 1999; also Olawsky 2000, 2002) analyses Dagbani as a tone language that additionally has predictable word stress, one main stress per phonological word, normally on the penultimate syllable (a small subset of words with final stress), cued by amplitude/duration rather than pitch — available to me only via snippets and reports. Native-speaker phonologists reject this: Hudu (2007, 2010) found no duration/intensity correlate and Hudu 2022 calls Dagbani 'a non-stress language' (with a trochaic bimoraic foot motivated by segmental phonotactics, whose head 'does not bear stress'); Inusah 2021 concludes Dagbanli 'is not stress marking'. The oldest description, Fisch 1912:3–4, put the 'Starkton' mostly on the antepenult, shifting to the penult when that syllable is heavy, and noted the stressed syllable always carries high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in the accessible sources; Riemer 2010 (summarising Olawsky 2002) speaks only of counting 'main stresses' per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: Per snippets of Olawsky 2002 (via Taylor ed. 2015:231): 'a subset of words with final stress'; Olawsky 2000: 'Heavy syllables do not automatically attract stress'. Fisch 1912: negative prefixes bi/ku and imperative -má attract the accent, infinitive -bu/-gu pushes it to the antepenult, adverbial yi- 'scatters' it over all syllables; compounding and suffix loss shift it.
new_statements.domain_note: Olawsky's stress is a property of the phonological word (used as his wordhood diagnostic: one main stress per p-word, incl. suffixed words and compounds). Hudu 2022's prominence is foot-level headedness (left-headed bimoraic trochee inside the prosodic word = root + inflectional suffix), explicitly not stress. All statements concern words in isolation; no phrase-level claims.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Dagbani (dagb1246). Inusah 2021 is explicitly cross-dialectal (Eastern/Tomosili, Western/Nayahili, Nanunli). Hudu's work draws mainly on the Eastern dialect. Fisch 1912 describes 'Dagbane' as spoken in North Togo and the northern Gold Coast (eastern Dagbon area, early 20th c.). Olawsky's data (1999/2002) are reported second-hand only.

[...] In stress languages, the primary indicator of headedness within the prosodic foot is stress. [...] In a non-stress language like Dagbani, headedness can only be determined using these other (non-prosodic) criteria.

new_statements.reading: Dagbani is a tone language without word stress: the leading present-day Dagbani phonologist treats it explicitly as a non-stress language whose left-headed moraic (trochaic) foot is diagnosed by segmental criteria only. This agrees with Inusah 2021: 157-158 (held by the project), which reports Hudu's 2007 acoustic finding that Olawsky's 'stressed' vowels are neither longer nor more intense and concludes 'stress does not exist in the phonology of the language'. The competing claim of regular penultimate stress (Olawsky 1999, 2002; the basis of the old StressTyp [P] label) was seen only in Google Books snippets. The earliest first-hand placement statement, Fisch 1912: 3-4 (held by the project), gives 'mostly antepenultimate, frequently penultimate with heavy syllables' but explicitly conflates stress with high tone. For a catalog entry, the defensible coding is 'no word stress (tone language); a penultimate-stress analysis (Olawsky 1999) exists but was refuted acoustically (Hudu 2007/2010)'.

new_statements.quote: Dagbani has contrastive tone, as observed by almost all researchers on the phonology. Olawsky (1999, 2002) is the first to claim that Dagbani marks stress in addition to tone. He claims that Dagbani stress is correlated with a higher amplitude and longer duration; distinct from tone, which is correlated with a higher pitch. In his observation, Dagbani stress systematically falls on the penultimate syllable. However, results of a phonetic study of one speaker of the Eastern Dialect, (Hudu 2007c), show that vowels that Olawsky claims to be stressed are neither longer in duration nor higher in intensity than vowels that are supposed to be unstressed. This supports the widely held view among many linguists (e.g. Larry Hyman, p.c.) that Dagbani and other Gur languages are not stress marking.

The next paragraph (pp. 19-20) describes the H/L tone system plus a contrastive falling tone in the Eastern Dialect, so the section is about Dagbani tone with stress explicitly denied: reading 'no word stress according to the source' is right. Bibliography p. 291 (p. 311…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Dagbani has an empty rule. Relative to existing_statements: agrees with the Hudu 2022 statement (non-stress tone language) and is the primary source behind Inusah 2021: 157's second-hand report; it refines by giving the actual wording and the experimental basis (one Eastern-Dialect speaker, duration and intensity measured) and by identifying the rebuttal as Hudu 2007c 'On the status of stress in Dagbani', UBC term paper, not the ultrasound qualifying paper (Hudu 2007a) named in the work's citation line. It contradicts the older penultimate-stress reading (Olawsky 1999/2002, van der Hulst & Goedemans 2010 snippet) that the existing statements already flag as refuted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dagbani is a tone language (H vs L, plus a contrastive falling tone in the Eastern Dialect) and does not mark word stress. Olawsky's (1999, 2002) claim of systematic penultimate stress (cued by amplitude and duration) is reported and rejected: a phonetic study of one Eastern-Dialect speaker (Hudu 2007c, UBC term paper 'On the status of stress in Dagbani') found the supposedly stressed vowels neither longer nor more intense than unstressed ones.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress at all per the author).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only other mention of stress in the dissertation (p. 119, Ch. 3) is a general remark about alignment constraints in stress languages, not about Dagbani.
new_statements.identity_note: Hudu 2010 p. 6 (p. 26): tone marking and other lexical details in the data 'reflect the Eastern Dialect, which is my native dialect' (Yendi area); the stress phonetic study (Hudu 2007c) used one speaker of the Eastern Dialect. Olawsky's penultimate-stress description is based on the Western (Tamale, standard) dialect. Nanuni is not represented in Hudu's data.

tone_statements.quote: In terms of tone inventory, Dagbani is similar to Dagaare with two contrastive tones— high and low (Hudu, 2010; Hyman, 1993; Hyman & Olawsky, 2004)—as exemplified below. (9) Minimal pairs H L dám ‘alcohol’ dàm ‘shake’ kpáŋ ‘guinea fowl’ kpàŋ ‘axe’ ... Dagbani is also characterized by the presence of contour tones (Olawsky, 1999). However, as in Dagaare, these contour tones do not function as independent minimal units as they are derived from the combination of level high and low tones, as in bâ ‘father’. This suggests that Dagbani, similar to Dagaare, is primarily a register tone language.
tone_statements.locator: p. 11, §3.2 'Tone in Dagbani', opening sentence with ex. (9) + p. 14, §3.2.1 'Tone-Bearing Unit in Dagbani', final paragraph
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive level tones, high and low, plus a downstepped high; syllable is the TBU; falling contours (bâ) are derived H+L, not units; floating L causes downstep; grammatical tone undocumented.

L tone verbs are underlyingly toneless: /to/, /zagsi/; not /tò/, /zàgsì/ b. H tone verbs have a H prelinked to the first mora only: /nyé, tábsi/; not /tábsí/ ... (27) Factors involved in determining surface verb tones in Dagbani a. underlying lexical tone (e.g. on verb roots: H vs. Ø) b. morphologically assigned tones (e.g. H suffix, LH pattern)

tone_statements.citation: Olawsky, Knut J. 1997. Interaction of tone and morphology in Dagbani. Handout, DGfS-Jahrestagung (19. Jahrestagung der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Sprachwissenschaft), Düsseldorf, February 1997. HTML handout on the author's Heinrich-Heine-Universität page.
tone_statements.quote: The tonal system of Dagbani has two distinctive tones, High (H) and Low (L). This can be shown by a number of minimal pairs which differ from each other only by pitch level. (1) <gballi> [gballI] (grave) H-H c.f. <gballi> [gballI] (zana mat) L-H <palli> [pallI] (road) H-H c.f. <palli> [pallI] (new) H-L - Distinctive tone occurs on vowels and nasals. - CV and N syllables bear exactly one tone H or L (no contour tones). - CVN or CVV syllables may bear two tones at the right word boundary.

readall_conflicts: One standing disagreement in the literature, not between the files opened today: Olawsky (1999, 2002, 2004; echoed by van der Hulst & Goedemans 2010 and the old StressTyp [P] label) describes regular penultimate stress cued by amplitude and duration, whereas Hudu (2007c as reported in Hudu 2010: 19; Hudu 2022: 274, 287) and Inusah (2021: 157-158) hold that Dagbani has no word stress and that Olawsky's stressed vowels show no duration or intensity difference. Fisch 1912: 3-4 gives mostly antepenultimate 'Starkton' but conflates it with high tone. Hudu 2010 sides with the no-stress position and is the primary account of the acoustic rebuttal; the rebuttal itself (Hudu 2007c) is an unpublished term paper whose measurements are described only second-hand (one speaker).

sources.quote: Ich beschränkte mich, die Silbe mit dem Starkton durch einen Akzent zu bezeichnen. Diese Silbe hat wohl stets den hohen Ton. Die stark betonte Silbe ist im Dagbane meist die drittletzte, doch bewirken die folgenden Silben, Präfixe und Suffixe, mannigfache Verschiebungen. Es scheint, wie im Griechischen, der Unterschied zwischen schweren und leichten resp. kurzen und langen Silben auf die Stellung des Akzents einen starken Einfluß auszuüben. Silben mit gedehnten oder auch mit weiten Vokalen, mit Diphthongen und ferner mit h, gb, kp, ny wirken als schwere, durch sie kommt der Akzent häufig auf die zweitletzte Silbe zu stehen.
sources.note: pp.3–4 'Töne': marks the 'Starkton' syllable with an accent; 'Die stark betonte Silbe ist im Dagbane meist die drittletzte' (mostly antepenultimate), but heavy syllables (long/open vowels, diphthongs, ŋ, gb, kp, ny) often draw the accent to the penult; some affixes attract or repel it (neg. bi/ku, imperative -má attract; infinitive -bu/-gu pushes it to the antepenult); the stressed syllable 'hat wohl stets den hohen Ton'.

tone.quote: As seen in (2), where forms are cited as they appear after the homorganic nasal infinitive prefix, Dagbani contrasts L and H tone verb roots. ... (14) a. L tone verbs are underlyingly toneless: /to/, /zagsi/; not /tò/, /zàgsì/ b. H tone verbs have a H prelinked to the first mora only: /nyé, tábsi/; not /tábsí/ ... (27) Factors involved in determining surface verb tones in Dagbani a. underlying lexical tone (e.g. on verb roots: H vs. Ø) b. morphologically assigned tones (e.g. H suffix, LH pattern)
tone.locator: Authors' MS (no page numbers): intro before ex. (2); ex. (14a-b); ex. (27a-b); published version pp. 97-108
tone.summary: Two tones, L vs H, contrast on verb roots (analysed as H vs toneless, default L); paradigm melodies H, LH; mora is the TBU; H spreading gives downstepped H and HL falls; floating L causes downstep.
